item.text: {"chapter_id":"6B","answers":[{"question_id":"6B.1","answer":"The record supports a genuine but incomplete welfare priority. Tshisekedi’s programme explicitly included education, universal health coverage, water, infrastructure and poverty reduction, and he directed 2023 budget priorities toward health, education and rural development (BATCH-0013-E007; BATCH-0023-E013). The government continued PDL-145T, planned substantial public financing for schools, health centres and local institutions, and reported free primary education and free maternity care as priorities (BATCH-0010-E004; BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0010-E006). There is some implementation evidence: the government reported construction underway and education-budget and teacher-pay increases (BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0022-E005). However, much evidence is official rhetoric, plans or reported milestones rather than independently verified execution; universal health coverage and free maternity care were still being implemented with acknowledged difficulties (BATCH-0008-E011; BATCH-0020-E012). Severe conflict, food insecurity, displacement and poverty remained widespread (BATCH-0020-E003; BATCH-0022-E013; BATCH-0010-E003), while the state’s militarized response generated serious civilian harm (BATCH-0009-E002; BATCH-0011-E018). Thus welfare was a stated and partly funded purpose, but it coexisted with security priorities, weak implementation and adverse outcomes.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E007","BATCH-0023-E013","BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0008-E010","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0022-E005"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0008-E011","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0020-E003","BATCH-0022-E013","BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0009-E002","BATCH-0011-E018"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Funding execution, service quality and national outcome attribution are incompletely documented.","Several positive claims come from presidential or governmental sources and may overstate delivery."]},{"question_id":"6B.2","answer":"There is evidence of expanded access in education and planned or partial expansion in health and local infrastructure. Free primary education was associated with millions of additional public-school enrollments by 2021–2022, and the government reported continued implementation in 2023 (BATCH-0014-E004; BATCH-0012-R01-E019; BATCH-0020-E012). PDL-145T began construction of schools and health centres, while government and UN materials identified free maternity and newborn care, family planning, displaced-children schooling and universal health coverage as active measures (BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0010-E006). Programme evaluations also found improvements in water and sanitation facilities and food-security services, though these were substantially implemented by WFP, UNICEF, FAO and partners (BATCH-0002-E001; BATCH-0002-E002; BATCH-0002-E003). Adverse evidence shows low sanitation and water access, nearly seven million children out of school, more than 2,000 schools closed in conflict areas, health systems at breaking point, and severe maternal-service access constraints (BATCH-0002-E002; BATCH-0022-E010; BATCH-0003-E013; BATCH-0008-E002). The Social Fund dissolution temporarily paused World Bank-financed services, and 2023 budget execution criticisms raise further implementation concerns (BATCH-0017-E002; BATCH-0024-E003; BATCH-0024-E004).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E004","BATCH-0012-R01-E019","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0010-E006","BATCH-0002-E001","BATCH-0002-E002","BATCH-0002-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0022-E010","BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0008-E002","BATCH-0017-E002","BATCH-0024-E003","BATCH-0024-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is little ruler-specific evidence on affordability, uptake, quality or equitable national coverage.","Donor and humanitarian contributions cannot be cleanly separated from government causation."]},{"question_id":"6B.3","answer":"The government adopted and reported several targeted protections: the Indigenous Peoples rights law, free maternity care, child-protection and reintegration proposals, gender-violence services, victim-reparation mechanisms, and education or social programmes directed toward women, children and vulnerable communities (BATCH-0001-E010; BATCH-0008-E006; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E006; BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0026-E009). PDL-145T was expressly framed as reducing spatial inequality, and the REDD+ distribution rules allocated shares to provinces and local entities (BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0024-E006). There are some reported outputs, including socioeconomic assistance to 9,500 women, judicial access for thousands and programme benefits for women’s food security (BATCH-0011-E006; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0002-E003). Nevertheless, exclusion and incidence remained severe: fewer than one percent of children with disabilities attended school, women and marginalized groups faced major participation barriers, displaced women and girls faced sexual violence and inadequate services, and hundreds of thousands were excluded from voting in conflict-held territories (BATCH-0011-E015; BATCH-0026-E010; BATCH-0008-E003; BATCH-0013-E011). Mining-related forced evictions and abuse further show failures to protect affected communities (BATCH-0010-E018; BATCH-0004-E002).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E010","BATCH-0008-E006","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0011-E006","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0026-E009","BATCH-0008-E010","BATCH-0024-E006","BATCH-0009-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E015","BATCH-0026-E010","BATCH-0008-E003","BATCH-0013-E011","BATCH-0010-E018","BATCH-0004-E002"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most distributional outcomes are localized, government-reported or donor-supported.","Reliable incidence data for poor regions, older people, minorities and disabled people are sparse."]},{"question_id":"6B.4","answer":"There was substantial formal staffing and administrative activity, including a cabinet reshuffle, judicial appointments, recruitment and training of magistrates, labour inspectors and judicial police, and appointments across service-related public bodies (BATCH-0009-E003; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0023-E017; BATCH-0009-E005; BATCH-0009-E004). PDL-145T used several implementation agencies and contracted firms, while World Bank-supported reforms emphasized procurement, competitive appointments and public-finance controls (BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0014-E002). Some institutional strengthening is therefore documented. However, qualifications, selection criteria, retention, staffing adequacy and performance are rarely demonstrated; the president’s appointment ordinances do not establish professional merit (BATCH-0008-E014; BATCH-0015-E006; BATCH-0019-E005). Service systems remained under-resourced, with insufficient judges, remote courts, weak labour inspection and inadequate health capacity (BATCH-0011-E005; BATCH-0023-E018; BATCH-0003-E013). Procurement and public-resource risks were material, including the allegedly altered Alfajiri tender, illegal concessions and budget irregularities (BATCH-0009-E007; BATCH-0001-E009; BATCH-0024-E004).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-E003","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0023-E017","BATCH-0009-E005","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0014-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0008-E014","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0019-E005","BATCH-0011-E005","BATCH-0023-E018","BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0009-E007","BATCH-0024-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Evidence concerns personnel and formal systems more than service-delivery performance.","The president’s personal role in procurement irregularities is not established."]},{"question_id":"6B.5","answer":"The administration created or used monitoring and evaluation mechanisms: the CPVS tracked presidential commitments, education authorities conducted a 2023 performance review, PDL-145T proposed citizen project monitoring, and budget law required indicators, reporting, internal controls and audits (BATCH-0020-E011; BATCH-0023-E006; BATCH-0023-E003; BATCH-0029-E004; BATCH-0029-E005). External partners also maintained monitoring teams and evaluated resilience programmes, while official audits exposed illegal logging permits and other governance problems (BATCH-0002-E004; BATCH-0001-E009). Tshisekedi convened a roundtable to assess the state of siege and publicly acknowledged implementation difficulties in health coverage and purchasing power (BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0015-E004; BATCH-0020-E012). Yet correction was limited or unverified. The CPVS and ministries often reported plans or self-assessed progress, while election observers found that audits and recommendations were not fully transparent or implemented (BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0013-E010; BATCH-0007-E010). Budget reviews identified incoherent spending, overruns and projects without visible field action, and social-fund restructuring paused beneficiary services (BATCH-0024-E003; BATCH-0024-E004; BATCH-0017-E002).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E011","BATCH-0023-E006","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0029-E004","BATCH-0029-E005","BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0001-E009","BATCH-0021-E012","BATCH-0015-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0013-E010","BATCH-0007-E010","BATCH-0024-E003","BATCH-0024-E004","BATCH-0017-E002"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is limited evidence of independent welfare evaluation followed by documented redesign or personnel correction.","Official monitoring claims are not consistently independently validated."]},{"question_id":"6B.6","answer":"The government took some preparedness and response measures: it coordinated with MONUSCO, EAC, Uganda and humanitarian actors, pursued ceasefire and disarmament plans, created patrols and protection arrangements, continued PDL-145T and free health measures, and supported ICC and transitional-justice processes (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0021-E002; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0010-E006; BATCH-0019-E001). Humanitarian partners delivered food, health, WASH, maternal and psychosocial services, with measurable local outputs, though these cannot generally be credited to Tshisekedi (BATCH-0025-E003; BATCH-0013-E015; BATCH-0013-E017; BATCH-0002-E010). Crisis outcomes remained extremely adverse: displacement reached about 6.8–6.9 million, food insecurity exceeded 25 million, schools and health services were disrupted, and sexual violence risks increased (BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0020-E009; BATCH-0022-E010; BATCH-0013-E014). The state-of-siege strategy failed to curb violence and was associated with serious abuses, while delayed assistance after Kwamouth and the Goma killings show avoidable protection failures (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0011-E001; BATCH-0011-E018). External armed groups, regional conflict, disasters and donor shortfalls materially constrain attribution (BATCH-0020-E010; BATCH-0016-E004).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0021-E002","BATCH-0016-E005","BATCH-0010-E006","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0025-E003","BATCH-0013-E015","BATCH-0013-E017"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0020-E009","BATCH-0022-E010","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E001","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0020-E010","BATCH-0016-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["National counterfactual evidence is unavailable.","Humanitarian outputs are often donor- or UN-led rather than ruler-directed."]},{"question_id":"6B.7","answer":"Formal safeguards existed in some domains: victim-reparation law provided legal aid, protection and compensation; budget law required transparency and controls; election directives prohibited exclusion and discrimination; and PDL-145T proposed public project monitoring (BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0029-E005; BATCH-0009-E001; BATCH-0023-E003). Some officials and security personnel were investigated or prosecuted, and Diongo was released without charge (BATCH-0011-E002; BATCH-0023-E014; BATCH-0003-E007). But practical political allocation and punishment remained a major concern. Authorities restricted opposition movement, demonstrations, journalists and critics; ruling-party supporters were implicated in violence; and election observers reported administrative-resource abuse, opaque voter-register processes and disputed tabulation (BATCH-0003-E001; BATCH-0003-E002; BATCH-0027-E002; BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0019-E013). Victims seeking compensation were reportedly assaulted, mining-affected communities lacked effective grievance mechanisms, and military courts imposed severe penalties amid allegations of selective or flawed proceedings (BATCH-0022-E009; BATCH-0010-E018; BATCH-0011-E021).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E002","BATCH-0029-E005","BATCH-0009-E001","BATCH-0023-E003","BATCH-0011-E002","BATCH-0023-E014","BATCH-0003-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E001","BATCH-0003-E002","BATCH-0027-E002","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0019-E013","BATCH-0022-E009","BATCH-0010-E018","BATCH-0011-E021"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index contains little direct evidence about welfare eligibility or appeals specifically.","Political favoritism is often inferred from institutional patterns rather than proven in individual benefit-allocation cases."]},{"question_id":"6B.8","answer":"The administration enacted or maintained several rights and dignity measures, including the Indigenous Peoples law, conflict-victim protections, gender-violence and reparation legislation, judicial access initiatives, and girls’ education and safer-school projects (BATCH-0001-E010; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0026-E009). UNDP-supported recruitment and mobile courts produced measurable justice outputs, and some police officers were arrested for protest abuses (BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0009-E005; BATCH-0002-E012). Equal dignity and remedy were nevertheless weak in practice. Discrimination against women, Indigenous peoples, minorities, disabled people and LGBT+ people persisted; fewer than one percent of children with disabilities attended school; women were underrepresented; and accessibility barriers affected older and disabled voters (BATCH-0002-E022; BATCH-0011-E015; BATCH-0026-E010; BATCH-0002-E023). Security forces used lethal or abusive force against peaceful demonstrators, journalists and critics, while mining evictions involved beatings, sexual assault and ineffective grievance mechanisms (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0025-E005; BATCH-0010-E018).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E010","BATCH-0029-E002","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0026-E009","BATCH-0009-E005","BATCH-0002-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E022","BATCH-0011-E015","BATCH-0026-E010","BATCH-0002-E023","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0025-E005","BATCH-0010-E018"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence is stronger for formal commitments and selected programmes than for nationwide remedies.","Some harms were committed by non-state actors, making presidential attribution uncertain."]},{"question_id":"6B.9","answer":"The administration pursued several potentially durable institutions: PDL-145T local infrastructure and administrative capacity, CPVS monitoring, universal-health financing mechanisms, the victim-reparation fund, judicial recruitment and training, and formal budget, audit and extractive-governance frameworks (BATCH-0010-E004; BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0020-E006; BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0029-E005). PDL-145T had government agencies, planned financing and a multi-year territorial design, while social-protection systems combined ministry responsibility with technical delivery agencies (BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0026-E005). Durability and resilience are uncertain. Many programmes remained under construction or dependent on donors; the Social Fund was dissolved and replaced with a pause in disbursements; health coverage and maternity care were still being materialized; and several child-protection institutions remained incomplete or weakly funded (BATCH-0019-E009; BATCH-0017-E002; BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0012-R01-E004; BATCH-0012-R01-E005). Conflict, weak staffing, corruption, judicial interference and opaque procurement further undermine institutional resilience (BATCH-0011-E005; BATCH-0028-E017; BATCH-0009-E007).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0029-E005","BATCH-0008-E010","BATCH-0026-E005"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0019-E009","BATCH-0017-E002","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0012-R01-E004","BATCH-0012-R01-E005","BATCH-0011-E005","BATCH-0028-E017","BATCH-0009-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The target period ends before long-term institutional survival or post-rule performance can be observed.","Reliable evidence on domestic financing, professional retention and operational independence is limited."]},{"question_id":"6B.10","answer":"The period contains some attributable or government-linked gains, especially expanded primary-school enrollment, free primary education, early PDL-145T construction, justice-sector staffing and selected humanitarian or social-service outputs (BATCH-0014-E004; BATCH-0012-R01-E019; BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0011-E006). The administration also maintained monitoring structures and introduced free maternity care near the end of the period, though later reported benefits cannot be treated as 2023 outcomes (BATCH-0020-E005; BATCH-0020-E012). However, ordinary people finished 2023 amid worsening or persistently severe insecurity, displacement, food insecurity, poverty, inflation and service disruption: more than 25 million faced crisis or emergency food insecurity, displacement approached seven million, inflation reached roughly 33.9% at year-end, and millions of children remained out of school (BATCH-0020-E009; BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0022-E008; BATCH-0022-E010). Conflict, armed groups, regional intervention, donor shortages and inherited state weakness complicate causation, but the government’s state-of-siege and militarized policies also failed to protect civilians and produced documented abuses (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0011-E018). The evidence therefore shows limited sectoral and institutional gains alongside severe, unequal and insufficiently durable life-chance outcomes.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E004","BATCH-0012-R01-E019","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0011-E006","BATCH-0020-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E009","BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0022-E008","BATCH-0022-E010","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E018"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Comparable 2019-to-2023, group-disaggregated outcome data are incomplete.","Some positive outcomes predate 2023 or depend substantially on donors and humanitarian agencies."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The strongest favorable evidence concerns education expansion, PDL-145T, formal social-protection and victim-rights frameworks, and monitoring or planning structures.","The strongest adverse evidence concerns conflict-driven displacement and hunger, unequal access, security-force abuses, weak remedies, politicized institutions and incomplete execution.","Attribution is clearest for Tshisekedi’s formal directives, laws, budgets, appointments and security-policy choices, but many service outcomes were shared with donors, UN agencies, provincial authorities, armed actors and external shocks.","Promises, budget allocations and institutional creation substantially exceed independently verified evidence of nationwide service quality, equitable uptake, correction and durable post-period effects."]}
